facts.statement: Aspidichthys is a large, shield-like placoderm fish with distinct bumps on its skin, found in marine deposits from the Upper Devonian period in the Eastern United States and Europe.
facts.quote: Aspidichthys ("shield fish") is a genus of large, distinctively tuberculated arthrodire placoderm of uncertain affinities from Upper Devonian marine strata in the Eastern United States and Europe.

facts.statement: The genus Aspidichthys was first described by Newberry in 1873.
Fossils of Aspidichthys date to the Frasnian stage of the Devonian period.
The thick bones of Aspidichthys are covered with an irregular pattern of large, rounded bumps.
facts.quote: The dermal surfaces of the thick bones are decorated with an irregular arrangement of large, rounded tubercles.

facts.statement: A 1938 restoration by Schmidt depicted A. ingens as having a large body, a small head, and enormous eye sockets based on a lost holotype.
facts.quote: In 1938, Schmidt made a restoration of A. ingens as a large-bodied, small-headed arthrodire with tremendous orbits after the now-lost holotype of that species.

facts.statement: The type species A. clavatus is known from fragments found in the Frasnian-aged Huron and Olentangy Shales of Ohio.
facts.quote: A. clavatus is the type species, and is known from distinctive fragments found in the Frasnian-aged Huron and Olentangy Shales of Ohio.

facts.statement: The median dorsal plate of A. clavatus measures between 39 and 44 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The length of the median dorsal ranges from 39 to 44 centimeters.

facts.statement: The species A. ingens is a very large variant found in Frasnian rocks in Germany, Poland, Morocco, and possibly Iran.
facts.quote: Aspidichthys ingens is a second, tremendously large species, known from Frasnian-aged strata of Rheinland, Germany, the Holy Cross Mountains of Poland, Moroccan strata, and possibly from Iran.

facts.statement: A. ingens possesses an 80-centimeter-long nuchal plate that is folded more steeply than that of A. clavatus.
facts.quote: The 80 centimeter-long nuchal plate is much more steeply-folded than that of A. clavatus.

facts.statement: According to Dennison (1978), A. ingens is the largest arthrodire known from Europe due to its massive nuchal plate.
facts.quote: According to Dennison 1978, the huge size of the nuchal plate makes A. ingens "the largest arthrodire in Europe."

facts.statement: The exact taxonomic classification of Aspidichthys remains uncertain among scientists.
facts.quote: The taxonomic relationships of the genus remain uncertain.

facts.statement: The relationship between Aspidichthys and holonematids is considered doubtful because holonematid dorsal plates are narrower, have a low keel, and lack a carinal process.
facts.quote: However, this relationship is also doubtful, as the holonematids' median dorsal plates differ from those of Aspidichthys by the former being more narrower, having a low keel, and having no carinal process.

facts.statement: Aspidichthys belongs to the parent group Arthrodira.
Aspidichthys is classified within the class Placodermi.
Aspidichthys lived from the Frasnian to the Famennian stages, approximately 382.31 to 358.86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Frasnian to Famennian (382.31 to 358.86 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Miles (1973) suggested Aspidichthys was related to Euleptaspidae, but this hypothesis was disproven because the proportions of the nuchal and median dorsal plates differ drastically.
rejected.quote: Miles, 1973, suggested the genus was related to the Euleptaspidae, though, this is disproved through noting the drastically different proportions of the nuchal and median dorsal plates.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'proportions of the nuchal and median dorsal plates'
